strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and previously open problem: designing a budget-feasible mechanism with provable approximation guarantees for submodular welfare maximization in procurement auctions, an important generalization beyond the classic valuation-maximization objective.

The technical construction (geometrically increasing threshold, singleton candidate with temporal protection, value-to-payment ratio parameter β, disjoint candidate sequences with owner indices) is novel and specifically engineered to overcome the core difficulty that the welfare objective can be negative and depends on private costs that cannot be directly queried.

The mechanism is shown rigorously to satisfy truthfulness (via obvious strategyproofness from the descending clock format), individual rationality, non-negative auctioneer surplus, and budget feasibility, with full proofs provided in the appendix.

As a byproduct, the paper obtains a new deterministic approximation ratio of 1/(12+4√3) for valuation maximization, a substantial improvement over the previous best deterministic ratio of 1/64 (Balkanski et al., SODA 2022), while also reducing runtime from O(n^2 log n) to O(n log n) — a meaningful independent contribution.

Experiments on large real-world social network datasets (up to hundreds of thousands of nodes) and a crowdsourcing/image dataset show consistent improvements in objective value and dramatic reductions in oracle query complexity and running time relative to baselines.

The theoretical analysis is detailed and self-contained, with careful partitioning arguments (Definition 4.2) and lemmas that isolate distinct sources of welfare loss, aiding reproducibility of the proofs.
weaknesses: The achieved approximation ratios for welfare maximization are quite small in absolute terms (0.0328 for general submodular, 0.0877 for monotone), and while they represent the first guarantees in this budget-feasible setting, the practical significance of such loose worst-case guarantees is unclear without further discussion of tightness or lower bounds.

The experimental comparison against Deng et al. (2025) baselines uses a post-hoc adaptation (truncating their unconstrained solutions to fit the budget) since those methods were not designed with budget constraints in mind; this truncation heuristic may understate the true best achievable performance of the baselines and could bias the comparison in favor of the proposed method.

The paper's experiments are restricted to two application domains (influence maximization and a crowdsourcing/image selection task); broader validation across more diverse submodular objectives or real procurement/crowdsourcing marketplace data would strengthen the significance claims.

No empirical or ablation study is provided to show sensitivity of performance to the choice of parameters α, β, ℓ relative to their theoretically optimal values, nor exploration of whether tuning them empirically could yield better practical performance than the values derived purely from worst-case theoretical analysis.

The paper's technique, while adapted to a new (harder) setting, builds heavily on established ideas from prior threshold-based descending clock auction mechanisms (e.g., Balkanski et al. 2022, Han et al. 2023/2025); the conceptual gap over these precedents, while real, is somewhat incremental at the level of individual algorithmic components even though the combination is novel.

The Impact Statement is essentially boilerplate and does not meaningfully discuss any limitations or potential negative/positive societal implications specific to procurement auction mechanisms (e.g., fairness among sellers, market power effects).
